  next: normalizeAddress

content.text:
VERDICT: CHANGES REQUESTED

The endpoint pieces are wired idiomatically — the exception, handler (matching `DuplicateHouseholdExceptionHandler`/`ProblemDetails` exactly), and YAML step insertion with `govern: [ transaction ]` all fit the existing conventions, and slotting the check before `build` is the right place. One structural issue:

**Duplicated "owners in this city" counting logic.** `CheckOwnerCityCapacity.service` computes:
```java
long inCity = ownerRepository.findAll().stream()
        .filter(existing -> city.equalsIgnoreCase(existing.getCity()))
        .count();
```
This is character-for-character the same computation already living in `AssignOwnerCustomerCode.service` (lines 24–26), which uses that same count to derive the per-city sequence number. The new class's own javadoc admits the coupling ("City membership is compared case-insensitively, matching how owners-in-city are counted in `AssignOwnerCustomerCode`") — a comment standing in for shared code. If one definition of "owners in this city" ever changes (e.g. trimming/normalizing city like the address normalization elsewhere), the capacity gate at 50 and the sequence numbering will silently disagree.

This codebase has an established idiom for exactly this: `CheckOwnerHouseholdUnique.sameHousehold` is factored out as "the single source of truth" and shared with `AssignOwnerHousehold` precisely so the 409 check and the assignment "can never drift." Follow that pattern here — extract the case-insensitive city count into one shared helper (a static method, or better a `OwnerRepository` query) and have both `CheckOwnerCityCapacity` and `AssignOwnerCustomerCode` call it — rather than duplicating the stream and relying on a javadoc note to keep them aligned.
